goldens.comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

per_golden_matches.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the same underlying problem as the golden comment. Both point out that the code assumes `content` is always populated when calling `.scrub` on it, but RSS feeds may not have content (only description or content:encoded), which would cause a nil error. adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/post.rb:132: raw_html returns externally sourced feed HTML unsanitized, enabling stored XSS through scripts, event handlers, and javascript: URLs when post.cooked is rendered

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, when cook_method is raw_html, the cook method returns `raw` directly without any sanitization (line 131-132 in post.rb). The raw content comes from RSS feeds via TopicEmbed.import which uses ruby-readability to extract content. While readability limits tags to 'div p code pre h1 h2 h3 b em i strong a img' and attributes to 'href src', this doesn't prevent XSS through javascript: URLs in href attributes. The content is then rendered with `raw post.cooked` in best.html.erb (line 18), bypassing Rails' HTML escaping. A malicious RSS feed could include `click` which would pass through readability's whitelist and execute when clicked. This is a real stored XSS vulnerability.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:49: open(url).read follows redirects without revalidating the destination, allowing an approved host to redirect requests to internal or private resources and cause SSRF

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in app/models/topic_embed.rb at line 49 where `open(url).read` is used. Looking at the diff, the code uses ruby-readability with `Readability::Document.new(open(url).read, ...)`. The `open()` function from Ruby's open-uri follows HTTP redirects automatically. While the code validates that the embed_url matches the embeddable_host setting (in topic_retriever.rb's invalid_host? method), this validation happens before the HTTP request. If the approved host returns a 301/302 redirect to an internal resource (like http://169.254.169.254 for cloud metadata or internal services), open-uri will follow it without revalidating the destination. This is a legitimate SSRF vulnerability - an attacker controlling content on an approved embeddable host could redirect requests to internal/private resources.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/topic_retriever.rb:26: the throttle key contains the exact user-supplied URL, so URL variations can bypass throttling and trigger unbounded feed polling, remote fetching, and topic-creation jobs

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in lib/topic_retriever.rb, the throttle key is constructed as `retrieved_key = "retrieved:#{@embed_url}"`. The embed_url comes from user input (params.require(:embed_url) in embed_controller.rb). The finding claims URL variations can bypass throttling. However, examining the code flow: 1) The invalid_host? check validates that the URL's host matches SiteSetting.embeddable_host, so only URLs from the configured host are processed. 2) While it's true that URL variations (like adding query params, fragments, or encoding differences) pointing to the same content could bypass the per-URL throttle, this is a legitimate concern but limited in impact since: the host must match the configured embeddable_host, and each unique URL would create a separate TopicEmbed record (checked in perform_retrieve). The throttle is per-URL which is intentional design - different URLs should be allowed to be retrieved. The real protection against abuse is the host validation, not the throttle. The finding overstates the issue - it's not 'unbounded' since host validation limits the attack surface significantly.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:15: embed URLs are stored and matched without normalization, so equivalent URL forms can create duplicate topics and split discussions

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in topic_embed.rb, the import method stores embed_url directly without any normalization (line 15: `embed = TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first`). The same URL can have multiple equivalent forms (e.g., with/without trailing slash, different query parameter orders, URL encoding variations, http vs https in some cases). The code does basic validation (`url =~ /^https?\:\/\//`) but doesn't normalize URLs before storage or lookup. This means 'http://example.com/page' and 'http://example.com/page/' would be treated as different URLs, potentially creating duplicate topics for the same content. This is a real correctness issue that could cause duplicate topics and split discussions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb:6: embed_url has the default 255-character string limit, causing imports of valid longer URLs to fail

adjudication.rationale: The finding points to a real issue. In the migration file db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb, the embed_url column is defined as `t.string :embed_url, null: false` without specifying a limit. In Rails, string columns default to 255 characters. URLs can legitimately exceed 255 characters (especially with query parameters, long paths, etc.). The code in TopicEmbed.import validates URLs with `url =~ /^https?\:\/\//` but doesn't check length, and TopicEmbed.import_remote fetches from arbitrary URLs. If a valid URL longer than 255 characters is imported, it would cause a database error when trying to save the TopicEmbed record. This is a real correctness/data integrity issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:65: URL absolutization mishandles document-relative and protocol-relative URLs, leaving the former relative to Discourse and incorrectly rewriting the latter onto the article host

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the absolutize_urls method in app/models/topic_embed.rb lines 52-70, the code checks if href/src start_with?('/') and then prepends the prefix. For document-relative URLs (like 'hello.html' without leading slash), they won't match start_with?('/') so they remain unchanged - this is a real bug as they'll be relative to Discourse's domain instead of the source article. For protocol-relative URLs (like '//cdn.example.com/image.jpg'), they DO start with '/' so the code will incorrectly rewrite them to something like 'http://eviltrout.com//cdn.example.com/image.jpg' - this is also a real bug. The finding correctly identifies both issues in the URL absolutization logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:49: remote fetch errors such as 404s, timeouts, and malformed responses are unhandled, causing indefinite embed reloads and potentially aborting an entire Disqus import

adjudication.rationale: Looking at app/models/topic_embed.rb:49, the import_remote method uses `open(url).read` without any error handling for network failures (404s, timeouts, connection errors, malformed responses). This is called from TopicRetriever.fetch_http and Jobs::PollFeed.poll_feed. If the remote URL returns an error or times out, the exception will propagate up. In the embed controller flow (EmbedController#best -> Jobs::RetrieveTopic -> TopicRetriever -> TopicEmbed.import_remote), an unhandled exception would cause the job to fail. The loading.html.erb page has a 30-second auto-reload, so if the remote fetch keeps failing, users would see indefinite reloads. Similarly, in the Disqus import (lib/tasks/disqus.thor), an exception from import_remote would abort the entire import process. This is a real correctness/robustness issue - network operations should have error handling.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/tasks/disqus.thor:147: using TopicEmbed.import_remote drops the imported thread's created_at, assigning root topics the migration time instead of their historical timestamp

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff in lib/tasks/disqus.thor, the old code at line 147 used PostCreator.new with created_at: Date.parse(t[:created_at]) to preserve the original timestamp. The new code replaces this with TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, t[:link], title: t[:title]), which only passes title as an option. Looking at TopicEmbed.import_remote in app/models/topic_embed.rb, it accepts opts but only uses opts[:title]. The import method it calls uses PostCreator without any created_at parameter. This means the historical timestamp from the Disqus import is indeed lost and topics will be created with the current migration time instead of their original dates. This is a real functional regression.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/tasks/disqus.thor:114: removing the --category/-c option without an alternative breaks existing import commands and prevents migrated topics from being placed in the requested category

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly shows the removal of the --category/-c option from the disqus.thor import task. Lines 117 and 144-148 in the original file handled category assignment, but these are removed in the new version. The method_option for category is deleted, and the code that looked up the category_id and passed it to PostCreator is gone. Instead, the code now uses TopicEmbed.import_remote which doesn't accept a category parameter. This is a breaking change for users who relied on the --category option to place imported topics in specific categories. Existing import commands using -c or --category will fail, and there's no alternative provided to specify a category for imported topics.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:35: existing embeds are revised only when the body hash changes, so title-only feed corrections do not update the topic title

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the import method in app/models/topic_embed.rb, when an embed already exists (lines 30-38), the code only checks if content_sha1 != embed.content_sha1 to decide whether to update. The update uses PostRevisor to revise the post content, but there's no code to update the topic title. The title parameter is only used during initial creation (line 21 with PostCreator). So if a feed item's title changes but content stays the same, the topic title won't be updated. This is a real functional limitation/bug in the code.
